lead: A state-variable filter wires a summer and two integrators into a loop. The summer output is high-pass, the first integrator gives band-pass, the second gives low-pass. The same circuit therefore supplies three responses at once, and adding them gives a notch. On an integrated circuit a switched capacitor driven by a clock replaces the resistor, so the cut-off becomes a capacitor ratio times the clock frequency. These filters sit in audio crossovers, anti-alias stages and tunable instrumentation where one accurate clock must set many cut-offs.
prereq: You need: the op-amp integrator, virtual ground and summing amplifier from Unit 6, and the second-order response and Q from Chapter 7.2.

sections.h3: The state-variable loop and its three outputs

blocks.text: Take an inverting summer, then two inverting integrators. Connect the second integrator's output back to the summer. Let both integrators use the same resistor R and capacitor C. Let V<sub>in</sub> be the input, and V<sub>HP</sub>, V<sub>BP</sub>, V<sub>LP</sub> be the summer, first-integrator and second-integrator outputs. Some syllabi call this the Kerwin–Huelsman–Newcomb (KHN) filter.

An inverting integrator with input x gives output −x/(sRC), where s is the complex frequency and RC is its time constant in seconds. Two such integrators invert twice, so the loop produces the standard second-order denominator s² + (k/RC)s + 1/(R²C²). Here k is the fraction of V<sub>BP</sub> fed back to the summer. Comparing with s² + (ω<sub>0</sub>/Q)s + ω<sub>0</sub>² gives the design equations.

blocks.where: f<sub>0</sub> is the centre frequency in hertz; R is each integrator resistor in ohms; C is each integrator capacitor in farads; k is the gain from the band-pass output back to the summer, a resistor ratio with no unit; Q is the quality factor, with no unit.

blocks.text: V<sub>HP</sub> is the summer output because a high-pass response falls at low frequency and the loop has not yet integrated it. V<sub>BP</sub> is the first integrator output: one integration of high-pass gives a band-pass shape. V<sub>LP</sub> is the second integrator output. The centre frequency f<sub>0</sub> is set by R and C only, while Q is set by k. Change k for Q without moving f<sub>0</sub>; change R or C for f<sub>0</sub> without moving Q.

sections.h3: Universal filter and the Tow-Thomas biquad

blocks.text: Because all three responses are available, the block is called a universal filter. A fourth op-amp can sum V<sub>HP</sub>, V<sub>BP</sub> and V<sub>LP</sub> with weighted resistors. Choose the weights so the high-pass and low-pass parts cancel at one frequency; the result is a notch (band-stop) at f<sub>0</sub>. This is how one chip can provide low-pass, band-pass, high-pass and notch outputs from the same tuning.

The Tow-Thomas biquad is another multi-op-amp form. It uses an input summer, two integrators and a feedback inverter. It also gives low-pass and band-pass outputs directly; a third input adds high-pass or notch. Its design also separates f<sub>0</sub> from Q, but the resistor names differ from the state-variable circuit. Only a few universities teach the Tow-Thomas by name; the state-variable loop is the one to recognise first.

Multi-op-amp biquads are used when a filter section must be tuned electronically. Replace the integrator resistors with voltage-controlled resistors or with switched capacitors, and one control voltage or one clock retunes f0. The cost is more op-amps, more resistors and a wider spread of component values than a Sallen-Key section from Chapter 7.2.

A resistor is hard to make accurately on a CMOS chip; a capacitor ratio is easy. Take a capacitor C, charge it to voltage V, then dump the charge into the next node every clock period T<sub>clk</sub> = 1/f<sub>clk</sub>. The charge moved per second is C V f<sub>clk</sub>, so the structure looks like a resistor.

blocks.where: R<sub>eq</sub> is the equivalent resistance in ohms; f<sub>clk</sub> is the clock frequency in hertz; C is the switched capacitance in farads.

blocks.text: Put this R<sub>eq</sub> into an integrator with feedback capacitor C<sub>i</sub>. The integrator's unity-gain frequency is 1/(2π R<sub>eq</sub> C<sub>i</sub>) = f<sub>clk</sub> C/(2π C<sub>i</sub>). The cut-off is therefore a ratio of two on-chip capacitors times f<sub>clk</sub>. Capacitor ratios match to about 0.1% on a chip, while absolute resistors may vary by 20%. The clock can be crystal-controlled, so the filter is accurate and tunable: change f<sub>clk</sub> and every cut-off moves in proportion.

The input must stay below f<sub>clk</sub>/2. The switched capacitor samples the input, so a higher input frequency folds down (aliases) into the passband. In a real chip an anti-alias low-pass filter sits before the switched-capacitor stage. Clock feedthrough and charge injection also limit dynamic range; those details belong to later courses.

figure.caption: The summer gives the high-pass output, the first integrator gives band-pass and the second gives low-pass; the dashed path closes the loop. Notice that one input feeds one loop and three outputs are taken at successive nodes.

spec.title: State-variable filter
spec.aria: A summer feeding two integrators in a closed loop, with the high-pass, band-pass and low-pass outputs taken at successive nodes.

examples.question: A switched-capacitor resistor uses C = 1 pF switched at f<sub>clk</sub> = 100 kHz. It is the input resistor of an inverting integrator whose feedback capacitor is also 1 pF. (a) Find R<sub>eq</sub>. (b) Find the integrator unity-gain frequency. (c) Show that this frequency equals f<sub>clk</sub>/(2π).
steps: Step 1. Convert C to farads: C = 1 pF = 1 × 10⁻¹² F.
Step 2. Convert f<sub>clk</sub> to hertz: 100 kHz = 100 × 10³ Hz = 1 × 10⁵ Hz.
Step 4. Unity-gain frequency f<sub>u</sub> = 1/(2π R<sub>eq</sub> C<sub>i</sub>). Here C<sub>i</sub> = 1 pF = 1 × 10⁻¹² F, so R<sub>eq</sub> C<sub>i</sub> = 1 × 10⁷ × 1 × 10⁻¹² = 1 × 10⁻⁵ s.
Step 6. f<sub>clk</sub>/(2π) = (1 × 10⁵)/(6.283185) = 15 915 Hz, the same value.
examples.answer: R<sub>eq</sub> = 10 MΩ and the unity-gain frequency is 15.9 kHz, equal to f<sub>clk</sub>/(2π).
examples.check:
import math
C = 1e-12
fclk = 100e3
R_eq = 1/(fclk*C)
f_u = 1/(2*math.pi*R_eq*C)
print(f"{R_eq:.1f}")
print(f"{f_u:.2f}")

traps: The summer output is high-pass, not low-pass. The second integrator output is low-pass; swapping them reverses the whole cascade.
Q falls as the band-pass feedback k rises. Do not use Q = k; the relation is Q = 1/k.
In a switched-capacitor filter the cut-off is not f<sub>clk</sub>. It is (C/(2π C<sub>i</sub>)) f<sub>clk</sub>, a small fraction of the clock.
A switched-capacitor input above f<sub>clk</sub>/2 aliases; the clock is a sampling rate, not just a tuning knob.
Do not compare an RC filter's absolute resistor tolerance with a switched-capacitor filter's capacitor ratio; ratio matching is the reason the switched-capacitor version is accurate.

quiz.q: Name the three outputs of a state-variable filter and the node where each appears.
quiz.a: High-pass at the summer output, band-pass at the first integrator output, low-pass at the second integrator output.

quiz.q: Why does changing the band-pass feedback gain k change Q but not f<sub>0</sub>?
quiz.a: k sets the damping term k/RC in the denominator, so Q = 1/k. f<sub>0</sub> = 1/(2πRC) contains only the integrator R and C, so it is independent of k.

quiz.q: Both integrators in a state-variable filter use R = 10 kΩ and C = 1 nF. Find f<sub>0</sub>. If k = 0.5, find Q.
A switched-capacitor filter is clocked at 100 kHz. A 60 kHz input tone appears at the output as a lower frequency. Explain.
quiz.a: The clock samples at 100 kHz, so the Nyquist limit is 50 kHz. The 60 kHz tone is above this limit and aliases to |100 − 60| = 40 kHz at the output.

quiz.q: A switched-capacitor integrator needs f<sub>0</sub> = 1 kHz. It uses C = 1 pF and C<sub>i</sub> = 10 pF. Find f<sub>clk</sub> from f<sub>0</sub> = f<sub>clk</sub> C/(2π C<sub>i</sub>).
Why is a switched-capacitor filter more accurate on an IC than an RC filter?
quiz.a: Its frequency depends on a capacitor ratio and a clock frequency. Capacitor ratios match closely on one chip, and the clock can be crystal-controlled. An RC filter depends on absolute resistor and capacitor values, which vary widely.
A filter block that provides low-pass, band-pass and high-pass outputs at the same time, and can also produce a notch by summing those outputs.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production audio codecs use fully differential switched-capacitor sigma-delta modulators because the same capacitor-ratio idea gives both the filter and the ADC. CMOS image sensors use switched-capacitor correlated double sampling to remove reset noise. Radio receivers use tunable biquads for channel selection. Search next for 'switched-capacitor biquad', 'anti-aliasing filter' and 'correlated double sampling'.
